questions.stem: Which two pieces of equipment can collect the gas produced in this practical?

options.text: A gas syringe or the downward displacement of water
options.explanation: Both capture the evolved gas for volume measurement, one by piston travel and one by water displacement.

options.text: A burette and a pipette
options.explanation: Those measure liquids in titration, not gas volumes.

options.text: A separating funnel and a beaker
options.explanation: Separating funnels split liquid layers; they do not meter gas.

options.text: A colorimeter and a cuvette
options.explanation: Those measure light absorption, unrelated to gas collection.

questions.stem: The model reaction in this core practical is between

options.text: Ethanol and ethanoic acid
options.explanation: That esterification makes no gas at all.

options.text: Sodium carbonate and hydrochloric acid
options.explanation: Na2CO3 + 2HCl releases carbon dioxide, the gas whose volume is measured.

options.text: Magnesium and steam
options.explanation: That reaction produces hydrogen but is not the practical's model here.

options.text: Copper oxide and carbon monoxide
options.explanation: That is a gas-solid reduction, not the carbonate-acid practical.

questions.stem: Why must the delivery tube be connected immediately after adding the sodium carbonate?

options.text: The sodium carbonate would dissolve the tube
options.explanation: No such chemical attack occurs.

options.text: The gas syringe needs warming before use
options.explanation: Temperature equilibration is not the issue.

options.text: Gas evolved before sealing would escape and understate the measured volume
options.explanation: The connection timing is the main defence against early gas loss.

options.text: The reaction would explode if left open
options.explanation: The reaction is a gentle fizzing, not a hazard requiring speed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption written into the method's validity?

options.text: The gas syringe has no scale markings
options.explanation: The syringe is precisely what carries the scale.

options.text: Carbon dioxide dissolves completely in the water bath
options.explanation: Dissolution would be a loss, not an assumption of the method.

options.text: The acid is added to the carbonate, never the reverse
options.explanation: The method adds solid to acid; the direction is stated as procedure, not assumption.

options.text: The reaction goes to completion before the volume is read
options.explanation: The method assumes complete reaction so the gas volume reflects all the carbonate added.

questions.stem: In the displacement-of-water arrangement, the gas volume is read from

options.text: The level of water the gas has pushed out of the inverted vessel
options.explanation: The gas displaces water whose volume equals the gas collected.

options.text: The mass lost by the reaction flask
options.explanation: Mass loss belongs to a different experimental design.

options.text: The colour change of an indicator in the water
options.explanation: No indicator is part of the collection.

options.text: The pressure gauge on the delivery tube
options.explanation: A simple displacement set-up has no pressure gauge.

questions.stem: State the equation for the model reaction of this core practical.
questions.modelAnswer: Na2CO3 + 2HCl gives 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, releasing one mole of carbon dioxide per mole of carbonate.

questions.stem: Name the two assumptions that protect the gas volume reading.
questions.modelAnswer: Negligible gas is lost between adding the solid and connecting the tube, and the whole set-up is airtight so no gas leaks.

questions.stem: Explain why the reaction is allowed to go to completion before the volume is recorded.
questions.modelAnswer: Only at completion does the syringe hold all the carbon dioxide the weighed carbonate can release, so a partial-reaction reading would understate the gas volume and corrupt every downstream calculation.

questions.stem: A student's set-up leaks around the bung. State the effect on the measured volume and on any molar volume calculated from it.
questions.modelAnswer: Both fall: leaked gas shrinks the recorded volume, and dividing the shrunken volume by the true mole count returns a molar volume smaller than the real one.

questions.stem: What is plotted on the axes of the mass-volume graph?

options.text: Mass on both axes, against itself
options.explanation: Plotting a variable against itself is meaningless.

options.text: Carbonate mass plotted horizontally and gas volume vertically
options.explanation: The manipulated variable goes horizontally and the measured gas volume vertically.

options.text: Volume on the x-axis and mass on the y-axis
options.explanation: The axes are reversed from the stated plotting convention.

options.text: Time on the x-axis and volume on the y-axis
options.explanation: Time belongs to rate experiments, not this mass-volume study.

questions.stem: How are anomalous results treated when drawing the best-fit line?

options.text: They are averaged into the line like any other point
options.explanation: Averaging in a bad point skews the fit.

options.text: The whole experiment is abandoned if any point strays
options.explanation: One anomaly does not invalidate the data set.

options.text: They are ignored so the line fits the reliable points
options.explanation: Discarding outliers prevents one bad reading from tilting the line.

options.text: They are circled and included with double weight
options.explanation: Outliers get no extra influence; they are set aside.

questions.stem: The molar mass of sodium carbonate used in the analysis is

options.text: 60.0 g mol-1, the carbonate ion alone
options.explanation: The carbonate ion mass omits the two sodiums.

options.text: 44.0 g mol-1, the carbon dioxide mass
options.explanation: 44.0 belongs to CO2, not the carbonate.

options.text: 23.0 g mol-1, one sodium only
options.explanation: Two sodium atoms ride in the formula.

options.text: 106.0 g mol-1, from 2 x 23.0 plus 12.0 plus 3 x 16.0
options.explanation: The summed atomic masses give 46.0 + 12.0 + 48.0 = 106.0.

questions.stem: The volume of gas must be converted from cm3 to dm3 before the final division because

options.text: Molar volume is quoted per mole in dm3, so the units of numerator and denominator must match the convention
options.explanation: Dividing dm3 by mol yields dm3 mol-1 directly, the standard quoting unit.

options.text: cm3 volumes are too small for any calculator
options.explanation: Calculators handle any magnitude; the conversion is about units, not arithmetic.

options.text: The mole only exists for dm3 substances
options.explanation: The mole is unit-free; the conversion serves the quoting convention.

options.text: Syringes only read in dm3
options.explanation: Syringes typically read cm3.

questions.stem: Using the worked data, 0.35 g of carbonate gives 79.0 cm3 of gas. The molar volume calculates to approximately

options.text: 7.9 dm3 mol-1
options.explanation: That drops a factor of ten in the conversion.

options.text: 23.9 dm3 mol-1
44.0 dm3 mol-1
options.explanation: 44.0 is carbon dioxide's molar mass, not the volume result.
106.0 is the carbonate's molar mass.

questions.stem: State the mole arithmetic used on the graph-reading mass.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbonate moles equal the graph-reading mass divided by 106.0, its molar mass in g mol-1.

questions.stem: State the final division that produces the molar gas volume.
questions.modelAnswer: Molar volume equals the gas volume in dm3 divided by the moles of carbonate, since one mole of carbonate releases one mole of gas.

questions.stem: Explain why the carbonate and the gas exchange in a one-to-one mole ratio here.
questions.modelAnswer: The balanced equation Na2CO3 + 2HCl gives 2NaCl + H2O + CO2 places a single CO2 against a single Na2CO3, so their mole ratio is one to one and the gas moles equal the carbonate moles.

questions.stem: A graph reading gives 0.50 g of carbonate releasing 118 cm3 of gas. Compute the molar volume and show the units of every stage.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles: 0.50/106.0 = 0.0047 mol; volume: 118/1000 = 0.118 dm3; molar volume: 0.118/0.0047 = about 25 dm3 mol-1, quoted per mole at room conditions.

questions.stem: A 0.950 g sample of a Group 2 carbonate releases 226 cm3 of carbon dioxide. What is the first calculation?

options.text: The molar mass of hydrochloric acid
options.explanation: The acid's molar mass plays no role in the deduction.

options.text: The mass of water formed
options.explanation: Water is not part of the gas measurement.

options.text: Moles of carbon dioxide, dividing 0.226 dm3 by 24 dm3 mol-1
options.explanation: The gas volume converts to moles first, feeding every later step.

options.text: The atomic mass of the metal directly
options.explanation: The metal mass emerges only after the mole count and subtraction.

questions.stem: Why must the carbonate ion's mass be subtracted before identifying the metal?

options.text: The carbonate ion is heavier than any metal
options.explanation: Carbonate at 60.0 is lighter than most metals; the reason is the subtraction logic, not a weight contest.

options.text: Carbon dioxide carries the metal's mass away
options.explanation: The gas is pure CO2; the metal stays behind in solution.

options.text: The metal is volatile and evaporates during the reaction
options.explanation: The metal ion stays in solution throughout.

options.text: The formula mass belongs to the whole MCO3, and the metal is only the part left after removing 60.0 of carbonate
options.explanation: Matching the full formula mass against a metal would mistake the carbonate package for the metal.

questions.stem: The worked deduction ends with calcium because the metal's mass calculates to

options.text: 40.9, closest to calcium's 40.1
options.explanation: 100.9 minus 60.0 leaves 40.9, and calcium at 40.1 is the nearest Group 2 match.

options.text: 100.9, matching calcium directly
options.explanation: 100.9 is the whole carbonate's formula mass, not the metal's.

options.text: 60.0, matching calcium
options.explanation: 60.0 is the carbonate residue, not the metal.

options.text: 24.3, matching magnesium
options.explanation: 24.3 is magnesium's mass, but the calculation gives 40.9.

questions.stem: Which protection is required when handling moderately concentrated acids in this practical?

options.text: A full hazmat suit for every acid
options.explanation: Protection scales with hazard; a suit is not the standard requirement.

options.text: Eye protection plus gloves, since such acids are corrosive
options.explanation: Corrosive acids demand both barriers at minimum.

options.text: No protection, since dilute acids are harmless
options.explanation: Even dilute acids can be irritant and need eye protection.

options.text: A fume cupboard only, with bare hands
options.explanation: Fume cupboards address vapours, not skin contact.

questions.stem: Concentrated nitric acid carries an oxidising hazard because it

options.text: Only reacts with metals, never with organics
options.explanation: The oxidising power targets combustible materials broadly.

options.text: Turns into water on contact with air
options.explanation: No such conversion occurs.

options.text: Can cause or intensify fires in contact with combustible materials
options.explanation: Oxidising acids supply oxygen to combustion, escalating fire risk.

options.text: Is too weak to damage skin
options.explanation: Oxidising hazard is an additional risk, not a sign of weakness.

questions.stem: State the relationship between moles of metal carbonate and moles of carbon dioxide in the acid reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: One mole of MCO3 releases one mole of carbon dioxide, so the gas moles equal the carbonate moles.

questions.stem: Name the three hazard classes acids can present in this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: Irritant when dilute, corrosive when moderately concentrated, and oxidising for some concentrated acids such as nitric acid.

questions.stem: Explain how the molar gas volume enters the metal-identification calculation.
questions.modelAnswer: The collected carbon dioxide volume in dm3 divided by the molar gas volume converts a measured volume into moles, and that mole count propagates through the carbonate to the metal's atomic mass.

questions.stem: 0.950 g of MCO3 releases 0.0094 mol of gas. Deduce the formula mass, the metal's mass and the metal, showing each subtraction.
questions.modelAnswer: Formula mass: 0.950/0.0094 = about 100.9; subtracting the 60.0 carbonate residue leaves 40.9 for the metal, matching calcium at 40.1 as the nearest Group 2 metal.
